summary: Pentoxifylline is a xanthine-derivative hemorrheologic agent indicated for intermittent claudication due to chronic occlusive arterial disease of the limbs. It and its metabolites improve blood flow by lowering blood viscosity and increasing red-cell flexibility, raising tissue oxygenation in the affected microcirculation. It is given as a 400 mg extended-release tablet three times daily with meals; benefit may appear in 2-4 weeks but treatment should continue at least 8 weeks. It does not replace definitive therapy such as revascularization. It is contraindicated after recent cerebral or retinal hemorrhage and in those intolerant to methylxanthines (caffeine, theophylline, theobromine). Bleeding (with or without concomitant anticoagulants/NSAIDs) and increased theophylline levels are notable risks.
indications: Treatment of patients with intermittent claudication on the basis of chronic occlusive arterial disease of the limbs

moa: Pentoxifylline and its metabolites improve the flow properties of blood by decreasing its viscosity, which increases blood flow to the affected microcirculation and enhances tissue oxygenation in chronic peripheral arterial disease. It produces dose-related hemorrheologic effects, lowering blood viscosity and improving erythrocyte flexibility, and modifies leukocyte behavior - increasing leukocyte deformability and inhibiting neutrophil adhesion and activation. The precise sequence leading to clinical improvement is not fully defined.

absolute: Intolerance to pentoxifylline or to methylxanthines (caffeine, theophylline, theobromine)
relative: Risk factors for bleeding (peptic ulcer, recent surgery)
monitor: Prothrombin time/INR if on vitamin K antagonists

preg: No evidence of fetal malformation occurred in animal studies, though increased resorption was seen at high doses; there are no adequate, well-controlled human studies (formerly Pregnancy Category C). Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Pentoxifylline and its metabolites are excreted in human milk. Because of tumorigenicity shown in rats, decide whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, weighing its importance to the mother.
renal: In severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min), reduce the dose to 400 mg once a day to avoid accumulation.
hepatic: Dosing information cannot be provided for patients with hepatic impairment; use with caution.

major: Vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) - increased prothrombin time/anticoagulant activity; monitor INR when starting or changing dose
Theophylline-containing drugs - increased theophylline levels and toxicity; monitor levels
moderate: Anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, NSAIDs - increased bleeding risk
Strong CYP1A2 inhibitors (e.g., ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine) - increased pentoxifylline exposure
Antihypertensives (including nifedipine, captopril) - small additive falls in blood pressure; monitor and reduce antihypertensive dose if indicated
minor: Beta-blockers, digitalis, diuretics, antiarrhythmics - generally used concurrently without observed problems
interactions.food: Take with meals; food helps limit GI side effects.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction described in the label.
interactions.diagnostics: May prolong prothrombin time when combined with vitamin K antagonists.

monitoring: INR if on vitamin K antagonists
Blood pressure in patients on antihypertensive therapy

missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember with food. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose - do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Symptoms are dose-related and may include flushing, hypotension, convulsions, somnolence, loss of consciousness, fever, and agitation (typically appearing 4-5 hours after ingestion and lasting about 12 hours). Manage with supportive care, gastric lavage, and activated charcoal; give special attention to supporting respiration, maintaining blood pressure, and controlling seizures.
